These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. - **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.

- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).

   park it wears *is* the in-review state and the failure park *is* the report (which
   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# A thin wrapper: every decision lives in the engine modules named in the `run:`
# lines below, which converge nightly — this file does not, so it must not grow
# logic. It carries no cron; the scheduler workflow's drain is the guaranteed
# delivery and a label event is latency sugar.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing here
    # decodes — so both ready spellings must appear for as long as any fielded
    # engine writes the legacy one (#1119).
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # A backstop against a wedged runner, well clear of any declared
    # `code_work_timeout`; the heartbeat's leash is what bounds real work.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:

          # below this never changes: `vars` is the context GitHub's own docs define as
          # non-sensitive and render unmasked in logs, so serialising it is not the
          # exfiltration shape that gets a workflow held for approval (#1336) — and this
          # file is the one path a converge cannot write, so keeping it independent of
          # what any task declares is worth a great deal. vars-bag.mjs is the reader.

          # worker then reads process.env.<NAME>.

    needs: execute

      actions: write
      issues: write

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Continue the drain, or escalate a chain that keeps dying

          CLAUDINITE_CONTINUATION_DEPTH: ${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}

2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
13	`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as `anything`).
14	On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
15	read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
16	`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
17	Whichever source it came from:
18	
19	- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
20	  applies to you.
21	- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
22	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
23	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
24	- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
25	  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
26	  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may
27	  land its PR only when the diff sits inside the policy, and the policy engine decides
28	  that, never your reading of the diff. Before step 2, run it from the repository root —
29	  `merge-policy.mjs` at the root of the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
30	  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`, falling back to
31	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` in the canon):
32	
33	  ```
34	  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
35	  ```
36	
37	  `AUTOMERGE: no` — leave the PR open for review, quote the verdict line in your wrap-up,
38	  and stop; a diff wider than its policy waiting for a person is a correct outcome, and
39	  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your
40	  branch's final commit to carry the arming trailer on its own line,
41	  `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy: <the same expression>`, push, and continue below (the
42	  `automerge-policy-scope` check re-measures the diff against the trailer, so a
43	  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).
44	
45	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
46	
47	`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
48	
49	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
50	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
51	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading an
52	  authorized landing to review is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
53	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
54	  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
55	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
56	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
57	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.
58	
59	## 2. Arm auto-merge
60	
61	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
62	it once this repo's required checks pass.
63	
64	## 3. When the arm is rejected
65	
66	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
67	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
68	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
69	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
70	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
71	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
72	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
73	  PR's **head sha**:
74	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
75	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
76	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
77	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
78	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
79	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
80	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
81	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
82	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
83	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
84	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the ceiling — the trail
85	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
86	    unseen check does not survive anything.
87	
88	## Never
89	
90	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
91	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
92	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
93	are always legal outcomes.
